title: Effect of filler particle size on the printability, physicomechanical and adhesion properties of highly filled experimental 3D-printed dental resins.
html:
Purpose: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of filler particle size on the printability, mechanical behavior, and surface properties of highly filled experimental 3D-printed dental resins before and after thermocycling.

Material and methods: Two highly filled experimental resins containing silanized barium glass with different particle sizes were formulated: microparticulated (1.5 µm) and submicroparticulated (0.7 µm). Specimens were additively manufactured by digital light processing and subjected to flexural strength (FS), elastic modulus (EM), Vickers microhardness (VHN), surface roughness (Ra), contact angle (θ), and shear bond strength (SBS) analyses before and after thermocycling (5000 cycles; 5°C-55°C). Printing time was also evaluated. Data were analyzed by independent t-test, 2-way ANOVA and Tukey tests (α=.05).

Results: The 0.7-µm formulation required significantly longer actual fabrication time than the 1.5-µm formulation (122.37 ± 12.10 versus 48.23 ± 2.96 min; p<.001). Before thermocycling, the 0.7-µm formulation showed significantly higher FS (p=.012) and EM (p<.001) but these differences were not maintained after aging. Thermocycling significantly reduced FS in both formulations (p<.001). The 0.7-µm formulation exhibited lower Ra and higher contact angle values than the 1.5-µm formulation, whereas no significant differences were observed for VHN or SBS. No significant formulation × aging interactions were detected for any evaluated property.

Conclusions: The 0.7-µm formulation showed higher initial flexural strength and elastic modulus and lower surface roughness. However, the mechanical differences were not maintained after thermocycling and no advantages were observed for microhardness or shear bond strength. These changes were accompanied by substantially longer fabrication time.

Clinical significance: Reducing filler particle size in highly filled 3D-printed resins may improve initial mechanical behavior and reduce surface roughness but these mechanical advantages were not maintained after thermocycling and were accompanied by substantially longer fabrication time.
